propositions.text: This is an application for judicial review of an Immigration Officer's decision dated June 26, 2019.
propositions.quote: This is an application for judicial review. The applicant, Ms. N.N. Soni, asks this Court to set aside a decision of an Immigration Officer made at the High Commission of Canada in New Delhi, India dated June 26, 2019.

propositions.text: The Officer refused Ms Soni’s application for a work permit.
propositions.quote: The Officer refused Ms Soni’s applicant for a work permit.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review application to set aside an Immigration Officer's June 26, 2019 decision refusing Ms Soni's work permit application.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons below, the application is dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review.

propositions.text: Ms Soni is an Indian citizen residing in Gujarat, employed as a senior bookkeeper, married with a teenage son.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni is a citizen of India and resides in Gujarat. She is employed as a senior bookkeeper with a firm in Gujarat, is married and has a teenage son.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni is an Indian citizen living in Gujarat, employed as a senior bookkeeper, married with a teenage son.

propositions.text: In November 2017, Ms Soni obtained a multiple-entry Temporary Resident Visa to visit Canada with assistance from a travel agent.
propositions.quote: In November 2017, Ms Soni obtained a multiple-entry Temporary Resident Visa (“TRV”) to visit Canada. A travel agent assisted Ms Soni to complete the TRV application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni obtained a multiple-entry TRV in November 2017 with travel agent assistance.

propositions.text: In September 2018, Ms Soni accepted a bookkeeping job offer in Pembroke, Ontario; employer obtained a positive LMIA valid until April 13, 2019.
propositions.quote: In September 2018, Ms Soni accepted an offer for employment as a bookkeeper with a company in Pembroke, Ontario. In October 2018, her prospective employer in Canada obtained a positive Labour Market Impact Assessment (“LMIA”) which was valid until April 13, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni accepted a bookkeeping job in Ontario and her employer obtained a positive LMIA valid until April 13, 2019.

propositions.text: Ms Soni travelled to Canada with family on March 26, 2019, arriving at Toronto Pearson Airport; they returned to India on April 29, 2019 as scheduled.
propositions.quote: On March 26, 2019, Ms Soni travelled with her husband and son to Canada, arriving at Pearson International Airport in Toronto. They were scheduled to return to India on April 29, 2019 and ultimately did so.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni and family arrived in Canada March 26, 2019 and returned to India April 29, 2019 as scheduled.

propositions.text: On arrival, Ms Soni’s husband told CBSA Officer their trip purpose was to visit Canada; they did not mention job offer, LMIA, or work permit application.
propositions.quote: On arrival at Pearson Airport, Ms Soni’s husband informed a CBSA Officer that the purpose of their trip was to “visit” Canada. Neither he nor Ms Soni mentioned her job offer, the LMIA, or a possible work permit application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni’s husband told CBSA their trip was to visit Canada, omitting job offer, LMIA, or work permit plans.

propositions.text: Within days of entry, Ms Soni visited immigration consultant who advised applying for work permit at nearest port of entry before LMIA expiry on April 13.
propositions.quote: Within days of their entry into Canada, Ms Soni visited the immigration consultant retained by her prospective employer. The consultant told her that her LMIA would expire just two weeks later on April 13 and that the best option was to apply for a work permit at the nearest port of entry.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni consulted an immigration consultant who advised applying for a work permit at port of entry before LMIA expiry.

propositions.text: On April 2, Ms Soni applied for work permit at Rainbow Bridge port but lacked required original documents; application refused.
propositions.quote: Following quickly-arranged medical examinations on April 1, Ms Soni and her family went to the Rainbow Bridge port of entry on April 2 to apply for a work permit. However, she did not have the required original documents she needed – she testified that she had no prior plan to apply for a work permit while in Canada, so she had not brought original documents with her. Without the originals, her application for a work permit was refused.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni applied for work permit April 2 without original documents; application was refused.

propositions.text: Ms Soni couriered original documents from India and returned to Rainbow Bridge port on April 10; medical info not yet in file.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni arranged for the original documents to be couriered from India. On April 10, she returned to the Rainbow Bridge port of entry with them. This time, the medical examination information was not yet in her file.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni returned April 10 with original documents but medical info was not yet in her file.

propositions.text: By April 11, medical documents uploaded; Ms Soni applied again at Peace Bridge port, was interviewed, raised concerns, withdrew application, and was authorized to leave Canada.
propositions.quote: By the next day, April 11, the medical documents had been uploaded. She applied again for a work permit, this time at the Peace Bridge port of entry. She was interviewed. During that interview, an Officer raised certain concerns about Ms Soni’s application, which caused her to withdraw it. At that time, she received a form authorizing her to leave Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni reapplied April 11 at Peace Bridge, was interviewed, withdrew application after concerns, and was authorized to leave Canada.

propositions.text: Peace Bridge Officer raised two concerns: (a) Ms Soni was untruthful on airplane declaration form about trip purpose; (b) TRV application stated zero education and housewife, conflicting with work permit application.
propositions.quote: According to Ms Soni, the Officer at the Peace Bridge (whom I will call the “Peace Bridge Officer” for clarity) raised two concerns during the April 11 interview: (a) Ms Soni was untruthful in completing the declaration form signed on the airplane during her flight to Canada (she ticked the box for Personal, not Business or Study, as the purpose of her trip to Canada); and (b) Ms Soni’s TRV application stated she had “zero education” and that she was a “housewife”, whereas her work permit application advised that she holds a Bachelor’s degree in Mathematics and is employed outside her home as a bookkeeper.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Peace Bridge Officer raised concerns about Ms Soni's untruthful trip purpose and conflicting education/employment info.

propositions.text: On April 12, Ms Soni’s LMIA was extended 30 days, allowing re-application; she and family returned to India April 29 as scheduled.
propositions.quote: On April 12, Ms Soni’s LMIA was extended by 30 days, enabling her to re-apply for a work permit. On April 29, Ms Soni and her family returned as scheduled to India.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni’s LMIA was extended April 12; she and family returned to India April 29 as scheduled.

propositions.text: On May 10 from India, Ms Soni applied online for LMIA-based work permit, spouse's open work permit, and son's study permit, including statutory declaration and supporting letters.
propositions.quote: On May 10, from India, Ms Soni applied online to the Canadian High Commission in New Delhi for a LMIA-based work permit, as well as an open work permit for her spouse and a study permit application for her son. Her application included a Statutory Declaration sworn in Canada and dated April 16, 2019, in which she explained the circumstances of her visit to Canada and addressed the concerns raised by the Peace Bridge Officer on April 11. The application also included a letter from the travel consultant who had prepared her TRV application containing the incorrect information, and an 8-page letter from her Canadian legal counsel in support of her application.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni applied online May 10 from India for work and study permits, including statutory declaration and supporting letters.

propositions.text: An Officer at High Commission refused Ms Soni’s work permit and related applications by letter dated June 26, 2019, citing subsection 200(1) IRPR.
propositions.quote: An Officer in the High Commission refused her application for a work permit and, consequently, the related applications for her spouse and son. The High Commission advised Ms Soni of the Officer’s decision by letter dated June 26, 2019. The letter stated that the basis for refusing the application was that the Officer was “not satisfied that you will leave Canada at the end of your stay, as stipulated in subsection 200(1) of the IRPR, based on the purpose of your visit.”

paragraphs.summary: The court states the High Commission Officer refused Ms Soni’s work permit and related applications June 26, 2019, citing subsection 200(1) IRPR.

propositions.text: Subsection 200(1) IRPR requires an Officer to issue a work permit if certain conditions are met, including that the foreign national will leave Canada at end of authorized stay.
propositions.quote: Subsection 200(1) of the IRPR provides that, in respect of a foreign national who makes an application for a work permit before entering Canada, an Officer shall issue a work permit if, following an examination, certain things are established. Paragraph (b) sets out the requirement that “the foreign national will leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for their stay …”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains subsection 200(1) IRPR requires Officers to issue work permits if conditions, including leaving Canada after authorized stay, are met.

propositions.text: Applicant raises issue that Officer’s decision is irrational and not justified by law or facts, relying on Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The applicant raises two issues. First, relying on Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, Ms Soni submits that the Officer’s decision is fundamentally flawed as being based on an irrational chain of analysis and not justified in relation to the relevant law and facts.

propositions.text: Officer based decision on irrelevant criteria, ignored contradictory evidence in Statutory Declaration, and failed to explain why concerns remained.
propositions.quote: She argues that the Officer based the decision on irrelevant and extraneous criteria, ignored evidence in her Statutory Declaration that contradicted the conclusion reached and failed to properly engage with and articulate why her sworn statement did not allay the Officer’s concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues the Officer’s decision is irrational, based on irrelevant criteria, ignored evidence, and failed to explain concerns.

propositions.text: Applicant contends Officer’s reasons are inadequate and unintelligible, failing to address evidence or explain refusal.
propositions.quote: Second, Ms Soni contends that the Officer’s reasons are inadequate. She submits that the Officer’s failure to address the evidence renders the decision inadequate and unintelligible. She argues that the reasons provide no insight into why the Officer refused the application.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant contends the Officer’s reasons are inadequate and unintelligible, lacking explanation for refusal.

propositions.text: Applicant argues procedural fairness required opportunity to respond to concerns about sworn statement to avoid veiled negative credibility finding.
propositions.quote: In the course of these submissions, Ms Soni argues that if the Officer had concerns about her sworn statement, Ms Soni should have been given an opportunity to respond as a matter of procedural fairness as to do otherwise would be a “veiled negative credibility finding”.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues procedural fairness required a chance to respond to concerns about her sworn statement to avoid unfair credibility findings.

propositions.text: Respondent submits Officer’s decision was reasonable and Ms Soni provided untruthful answers to immigration authorities on two occasions.
propositions.quote: The respondent’s position is that the Officer’s decision was reasonable. The Minister submits that Ms Soni provided untruthful answers – lies – to Canadian immigration authorities on two separate occasions.

propositions.text: Respondent argues untruthfulness is a reasonable ground to deny work permit, citing Porfirio and Chamma cases.
propositions.quote: Regardless of the explanations she provided with her application, the respondent contends that a finding that the applicant was not truthful is a reasonable reason for denying an application for a work permit: Porfirio v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 794 (Near, J.); Chamma v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 29 (Shore, J.).

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues the Officer’s decision was reasonable due to Ms Soni’s untruthful answers, citing precedent supporting denial for untruthfulness.

propositions.text: Officers rely on prior interactions with immigration officials to assess likelihood of future compliance.
propositions.quote: when Officers make decisions about whether an applicant will leave Canada at the end of their permitted stay, evidence of prior interactions with immigration officials are the best indicators of an applicant’s likelihood of future compliance.

propositions.text: Officer reasonably weighed applicant's past conduct over her explanations for misstatements.
propositions.quote: The Officer chose to weigh the applicant’s past conduct and other factors over the various explanations provided by the applicant to explain her misstatements, and made a reasonable finding.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues Officers reasonably rely on prior interactions and weighed applicant's past conduct over her explanations for misstatements.

propositions.text: Adequacy of reasons is not a standalone ground to set aside decision; decision is clear and reasonable.
propositions.quote: the respondent submits that adequacy of reasons is not a standalone reason for setting aside a decision and that the decision is “clear and reasonable”.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent submits adequacy of reasons alone does not justify setting aside decision, which is clear and reasonable.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is the presumed standard for judicial review of administrative decisions.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness is the presumed standard applicable to judicial review of administrative decisions.

propositions.text: Presumption of reasonableness can be rebutted by legislative intent or rule of law exceptions.
propositions.quote: The presumption may be rebutted by legislative intent, or if the rule of law requires a different standard: Vavilov, at paras 17, 23 and 69.

propositions.text: Only five exceptions to reasonableness standard exist, none apply here.
propositions.quote: Vavilov identifies only five such situations: see Entertainment Software Association v. Society of Composers, Authors and Music Publishers of Canada, 2020 FCA 100 (Stratas, JA), at para 16. None of those exceptions applies here.

paragraphs.summary: Court states reasonableness is presumed standard for judicial review, with limited exceptions none apply here.

propositions.text: Parties agree and court finds reasonableness is the standard of review for Officer's decision.
propositions.quote: The parties both submit, and I agree, that the standard of review of the Officer’s decision in this matter is reasonableness.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with parties that reasonableness is the standard of review for Officer's decision.

propositions.text: Reasonable decision must have coherent, rational analysis and be justified by facts and law.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is one that is: (a) based on an internally coherent and a rational chain of analysis and (b) justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision-maker: Vavilov, at para 85.

propositions.text: Decision reached on improper basis or unreasonable analysis is not reasonable.
propositions.quote: An otherwise reasonable outcome will not stand if it was reached on an improper basis, for example by an unreasonable chain of analysis in the reasons, or if the decision is not justified in relation to the facts and applicable law: Vavilov, at paras 83-86 and 96-97; Delta Air Lines Inc. v. Lukács, 2018 SCC 2, [2018] 1 S.C.R. 6.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains reasonableness requires coherent analysis justified by facts and law; improper basis or analysis negates reasonableness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review is robust but disciplined, requiring serious shortcomings to intervene.
propositions.quote: Reasonableness review entails a sensitive and respectful, but robust, evaluation of administrative decisions: Vavilov at paras 12-13.

propositions.text: Flaws must be fundamental or significant, not minor or superficial, to render decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Flaws or shortcomings must be more than superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision, or a “minor misstep”. The problem must be sufficiently fundamental or significant to render the decision unreasonable: para 100.

paragraphs.summary: Court states reasonableness review is robust but requires fundamental flaws to intervene, not minor errors.

propositions.text: Two fundamental flaws: internal irrationality or untenability given factual and legal constraints.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court in Vavilov, at paragraph 101, identified two types of fundamental flaws: a failure of rationality internal to the reasoning process in the decision; and when a decision is in some respect untenable in light of the relevant factual and legal constraints that bear on it.

propositions.text: Reviewing court may consider evidence as factual constraint but must not reweigh evidence.
propositions.quote: However, the reviewing court must not reweigh or reassess the evidence: Vavilov, at paras 125-126.

paragraphs.summary: Court explains fundamental flaws are irrationality or untenability; court may consider evidence but not reweigh it.

propositions.text: Reviewing court may consider parties' submissions as decision-maker must address central issues raised.
propositions.quote: the reviewing court may consider the submissions of the parties to the decision-maker, because the decision-maker’s reasons must meaningfully account for the central issues and concerns raised by the parties: Vavilov, at para 127.

propositions.text: Decision-maker need not respond to every argument but failure to address key issues may question alertness to matter.
propositions.quote: a decision-maker’s failure to meaningfully grapple with key issues or central arguments raised by the parties “may call into question whether the decision-maker was actually alert and sensitive to the matter before it.” Vavilov, at para 128.

paragraphs.summary: Court states reviewing court may consider parties' submissions; failure to address key issues questions decision-maker's alertness.

propositions.text: Standard of review for procedural fairness is correctness with no deference.
propositions.quote: the applicant states that the standard of review is correctness.

propositions.text: Judicial review of procedural fairness involves no deference; question is if party had full and fair chance to respond.
propositions.quote: judicial review of procedural fairness involves no margin of appreciation or deference by a reviewing court. The ultimate question is whether the party affected knew the case to meet and had a full and fair or meaningful chance to respond

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues procedural fairness standard is correctness; court agrees no deference applies, focus on fair chance to respond.

propositions.text: Officer's decision was reasonable, with no fundamental flaw or untenability given evidence and submissions.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s decision was reasonable. It does not contain a fundamental flaw in its overarching logic and is not untenable in view of the evidence and the submissions made by Ms Soni.

propositions.text: Conclusion under IRPR paragraph 200(1)(b) was open to Officer based on evidence.
propositions.quote: The conclusion reached under IRPR paragraph 200(1)(b) was open to the Officer based on the evidence.

propositions.text: Officer's reasons are adequate and decision sufficiently transparent, intelligible and justified despite not containing every point a court might expect.
propositions.quote: The reasons for denying the work permit are adequate and overall, the Officer’s decision is sufficiently transparent, intelligible and justified.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer's decision reasonable, adequately justified, and open on evidence under IRPR 200(1)(b).

propositions.text: Applicant challenges Officer's decision focusing on passage about discrepancies, migration history, and family travel.
propositions.quote: In essence, they focus on the following passage in the Officer’s entry in the Global Case Management System: … given the discrepancies and contradictions between the applicant’s TRV [Temporary Resident Visa] application and her current stated employment history, while considering her migration history and repeated attempts to obtain a WP [work permit] at the border while on a TRV, and in light of the fact that the whole family would travel together, I am not satisfied …

paragraphs.summary: Applicant challenges Officer's decision focusing on passage about discrepancies, migration history, and family travel.

propositions.text: Discrepancies were inadvertent errors for which travel consultant took responsibility.
propositions.quote: the “discrepancies and contradictions between the applicant’s TRV application and her current stated employment history”, were “inadvertent and honest errors” for which Ms Soni’s travel consultant (who prepared the TRV application) has taken full responsibility;

propositions.text: Migration history and repeated work permit attempts were lawful and explained in Statutory Declaration.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni’s “migration history and repeated attempts to obtain a WP at the border while on a TRV”, were explained in her Statutory Declaration and were all lawful.

propositions.text: Officer ignored evidence explaining why applicant said purpose was 'visit' and gave reasonable explanation for multiple work permit attempts.
propositions.quote: She contends that the Officer ignored her evidence about why she and her husband advised the border Officer on March 26 that the purpose of their trip to Canada was to “visit”. She also contends that she provided a reasonable explanation for her multiple attempts to obtain a work permit at the border that squarely contradicts the conclusion of the Officer.

propositions.text: Lawful efforts should favor application; negative inference is unreasonable per Campbell Hara case.
propositions.quote: According to Ms Soni, these lawful efforts should have favoured her application, no negative inference can be drawn against her, and to do so is unreasonable according to Campbell Hara v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 263 (Russell, J.);

propositions.text: Family traveling together is no basis for negative inference against applicant.
propositions.quote: and (iii) the fact that the “whole family would travel together” is no basis for a negative inference against her.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues discrepancies were inadvertent, migration history lawful, Officer ignored explanations, lawful efforts favor application, family travel no negative inference.

propositions.text: Officer failed to explicitly and meaningfully engage with explanations and evidence in Statutory Declaration.
propositions.quote: the applicant contends that the Officer failed to engage explicitly and meaningfully with the explanations and evidence in Ms Soni’s Statutory Declaration.

propositions.text: Applicant deserved a decision considering all submitted materials, which was not done.
propositions.quote: the “applicant deserved a decision that considered the entirety of her submitted materials. This was not done.”

paragraphs.summary: Applicant contends Officer failed to meaningfully engage with evidence and did not consider all submitted materials.

propositions.text: Reviewing court must consider decision as a whole, not just isolated passages.
propositions.quote: a reviewing court look at the decision as a whole – not just a few lines or a particular passage (at paras 15, 85, 99 and 102).

propositions.text: Fundamental logic or key reasoning may be captured in a passage but wider reasoning must be considered with outcome.
propositions.quote: That is not to say that the fundamental logic or key reasoning in a decision may not be captured in a particular passage – it often is. But the wider arc of reasoning, including the decision-maker’s appreciation of the circumstances in the particular case, must be considered together with the overall outcome.

paragraphs.summary: Court states reviewing court must consider decision as whole, including wider reasoning and outcome, not just passages.

propositions.text: Vavilov requires reviewing judge to consider both reasons and overall outcome.
propositions.quote: the reviewing judge must consider both the reasons provided by decision-maker and the overall outcome (at paras 83 and 87).

propositions.text: Reasons are primary mechanism showing decision reasonableness; close attention required.
propositions.quote: The reviewing court should start with the reasons, as they are the “primary mechanism by which administrative decision-makers show that their decisions are reasonable” (at para 81). “[C]lose attention” must be paid to those reasons (at para 97).

paragraphs.summary: Court explains Vavilov requires considering reasons and outcome; reasons are primary mechanism showing reasonableness.

propositions.text: Justification requirements must consider context and impact on individual rights and interests.
propositions.quote: the legal requirements for justification cannot lose sight of the specific context in which the impugned decision arises. The decision must be responsive to those affected by it, particularly if the impact of the decision on the individual’s rights and interests is severe: Vavilov, at paras 86 and 133.

propositions.text: Judicial review must be mindful of legal context of impugned decision.
propositions.quote: Judicial review of the decision must also be mindful of the legal context of the impugned decision: Vavilov, at paras 86 and 89-94.

paragraphs.summary: Court states justification must consider context and impact on rights; judicial review mindful of legal context.

propositions.text: Applicant is foreign national applying from outside Canada; application significant to her and family.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni is a foreign national who applied from outside Canada for a work permit. The application was naturally of significance in the minds of Ms Soni and her family

propositions.text: Impact of Officer’s decision on applicant’s rights and interests cannot be characterized as severe.
propositions.quote: the impact of the Officer’s decision on her rights and interests (if any) cannot be characterized as severe: Sharma v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 381 (Gascon, J.), at para 32; Chhetri v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 872 (Rennie, J.), at paras. 9-10; Qin v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2002 FCT 815 (Rothstein, JA), at para. 5.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds applicant is foreign national; impact of decision on her rights is not severe.

propositions.text: Officer’s decision focused on applicant’s truthfulness affecting likelihood to leave Canada under IRPR 200(1)(b).
propositions.quote: the Officer’s decision resolved to a focal point – Ms Soni’s truthfulness in her dealings with Canadian immigration officials – which directly affected the Officer’s determination about whether she, as a foreign national, would leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for her stay under IRPR paragraph 200(1)(b).

propositions.text: Officer not required to write extended reasons analyzing every nuance or legal argument to meet justification requirements.
propositions.quote: the Court’s reasoning in Vavilov did not require the Officer at the High Commission to write extended reasons examining each nuance of Ms Soni’s work permit application, or analyzing every nook and cranny of her counsel’s legal argument, in order to comply with the requirements of justification, transparency and intelligibility in our administrative law: Vavilov, at para 128.

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Officer focused on applicant's truthfulness; extended reasons not required to meet justification standards.

propositions.text: Applicant’s Statutory Declaration detailed background, purpose, arrival, visits, applications, concerns, explanations, education, work history, and LMIA extension.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni first set out the background and her purpose(s) in coming to Canada in March 2019 (at paras 1-6 and 8-9). She described her arrival at the airport (at para 7) and her visit with the immigration consultant and the medical appointments on April 1 (at paras 10-12). She explained her applications at the ports of entry from April 2 to April 11, the concerns raised by the Peace Bridge Officer on April 11 and her reaction (at paras 12-24, 29, 37-38 and 40-43). She also describes her explanations and responses to those concerns through her immediate contact with the travel agent who prepared her TRV application (at paras 25-28 and 30-31) and her actual education and work history (at paras 32-36). She also noted the extension of her LMIA (at para 39).

paragraphs.summary: Court summarizes contents of applicant's Statutory Declaration detailing background, visits, applications, concerns, and work history.

propositions.text: Applicant’s legal counsel submitted detailed letter with employment, education, immigration history, legal submissions, and supporting documents.
propositions.quote: Her Canadian legal counsel integrated this content, and much more, into their letter to the High Commission dated May 10, 2019 that was included with her application for a work permit. Over eight single-spaced pages, the letter set out in detail: the proposed employment position in Pembroke (at pp. 1-2); Ms Soni’s education and work experience (at p. 2); Ms Soni’s immigration history – which included the discussion with the border Officer at the airport, her applications at the ports of entry, the concerns raised by the Officer, and the travel agent having taken “full responsibility for the incorrect information” as a result of “their errors” (underlined and bolded in both cases) (at pp. 2-4); Legal Submissions under the general heading “Ms Soni is not inadmissible for misrepresentation” and the subheadings “Ms Soni’s inadvertent errors in her application forms” and “Ms Soni’s genuine intention to enter as a visitor”. These submissions on pp. 4-6 included specific case law from this Court with block quotations; Accompanying Dependents (at pp. 6-7); and A list of the twenty Supporting Documents, including the Statutory Declaration (at pp. 7-8).

paragraphs.summary: Court describes detailed letter from applicant’s counsel with employment, education, immigration history, legal submissions, and supporting documents.

propositions.text: Ms Soni's legal counsel advocated her position and explanations responding to two truthfulness concerns raised by the Peace Bridge Officer on April 11.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni’s legal counsel set out and advocated for her position overall and specifically for her explanations in response to the two truthfulness concerns raised by the Peace Bridge Officer on April 11.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms Soni's legal counsel advocated her position and explanations responding to two truthfulness concerns raised by the Peace Bridge Officer on April 11.

propositions.text: Ms Soni did not deny inconsistencies between her TRV application and work permit application.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni did not deny that there were inconsistencies between her TRV application and her work permit.

propositions.text: Ms Soni claimed she trusted the travel consultant and signed the application as instructed.
propositions.quote: she put her “whole trust and belief” in the travel consultant and simply signed and dated the application as the consultant instructed.

propositions.text: Legal counsel described the inconsistencies as a mistake and administrative error by the consultant.
propositions.quote: Her legal counsel’s letter characterized it as a “mistake and honest error” and an “administrative error” by the consultant

propositions.text: Consultant's letter attached to work permit application took responsibility for errors.
propositions.quote: Her work permit application attached a short letter from the consultant that appears to take responsibility for the errors.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Ms Soni admitted inconsistencies in her applications, blamed the consultant, and counsel called it an honest error.

propositions.text: Ms Soni claimed she had no chance to explain arrival details and no non-disclosure problem existed.
propositions.quote: she claimed she had no opportunity to offer details on her arrival at the border on March 26 and that, in any event, there was no non-disclosure problem

propositions.text: Ms Soni said the trip purpose was to visit Canada and check schools for her son.
propositions.quote: in our minds, coming to see Canada and to check on schools etc prior to making an application was to visit

propositions.text: Ms Soni testified her primary reason was to see Canada and schools for her son during holidays.
propositions.quote: my primary reason for coming to Canada was to see Canada especially the schools for my son Viren

propositions.text: She said if suitable, they would decide on work and study permits while husband returned to India.
propositions.quote: if we found it suitable, we could then make a decision as to applying for my work permit and Viren’s study permit

propositions.text: Her LMIA had dual intent: work permit and permanent residency support.
propositions.quote: her LMIA had a dual intent – both for the work permit and to support her permanent residency.

propositions.text: Counsel's letter reinforced that the trip was a visit and no misrepresentation occurred.
propositions.quote: Her counsel’s letter to the High Commission reinforces her position that the purpose of the trip was to visit and that no misrepresentation occurred

paragraphs.summary: Ms Soni argued she had no chance to explain arrival, trip was a visit to check schools, and no misrepresentation occurred, supported by counsel.

propositions.text: Did the Officer fail to engage sufficiently with Ms Soni’s explanations to make the decision unreasonable?
propositions.quote: Did the Officer fail to engage sufficiently with Ms Soni’s explanations just described, so as to make the Officer’s decision unreasonable?

paragraphs.summary: The court asks if the Officer failed to engage sufficiently with Ms Soni's explanations making the decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Officer was aware of material events and Ms Soni’s position on them from GCMS Notes.
propositions.quote: It is clear from a closer review of the GCMS Notes that the Officer was aware of both the events material to the determination ... and Ms Soni’s position on them.

propositions.text: The explanation will focus on the challenged 'operative' passage in the Officer’s GCMS Notes.
propositions.quote: I will organize the explanation that follows around the ‘operative’ passage whose reasoning the applicant has challenged on this application.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer knew material events and Ms Soni’s position, focusing on the challenged 'operative' passage in GCMS Notes.

propositions.text: The 'operative' passage has three elements and is part of broader GCMS Notes.
propositions.quote: The ‘operative’ passage and its three elements do not stand alone in the Officer’s GCMS Notes.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes described discrepancies between TRV application and current employment history.
propositions.quote: GCMS Notes had already described the “discrepancies and contradictions between the applicant’s TRV application and her current stated employment history”

propositions.text: TRV application said housewife with no education experience; letters showed employment as bookkeeper and other company.
propositions.quote: on her previous TRV application, [Ms Soni] declared being housewife and having no education experience. One letter of employment indicates that [she] was employed as Bookkeeper ... Another letter indicates that [she] worked for another company

propositions.text: No pay stubs provided but salary certificates on file; discrepancies raised concern.
propositions.quote: No pay stubs have been provided but salary certificates are on file. The discrepancy ... raise concern.

propositions.text: Officer noted reading counsel’s letter but concerns remained.
propositions.quote: I have noted and considered the submission from the applicant’s representative, however, my concerns remain.

propositions.text: Counsel agreed this sentence refers to their May 10, 2019 letter to High Commission.
propositions.quote: Counsel for Ms Soni agreed at the hearing that this sentence refers to her legal counsel’s comprehensive letter to the High Commission dated May 10, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Officer’s GCMS Notes detailed discrepancies in Ms Soni’s applications and that concerns remained despite counsel’s letter.

propositions.text: Officer was aware and concerned about inconsistencies in Ms Soni’s original application and corrected facts in work permit application.
propositions.quote: The Officer was clearly aware of and concerned about the inconsistencies in Ms Soni’s original application ... and the corrected facts about her education and employment history

propositions.text: Officer read counsel’s letter containing Ms Soni’s explanations but concerns remained.
propositions.quote: Despite having read her counsel’s letter, which contained Ms Soni’s explanations, the Officer’s concerns remained.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer knew of inconsistencies and read counsel’s explanations but remained concerned.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes described Ms Soni’s migration history and repeated work permit attempts at border while on TRV.
propositions.quote: the Officer’s GCMS Notes had already described Ms Soni’s “migration history and repeated attempts to obtain a WP at the border while on a TRV”

propositions.text: Officer noted Ms Soni’s entry on March 26 without disclosing employment prospects.
propositions.quote: The Officer noted Ms. Soni’s original entry into Canada on March 26, “not disclosing her employment prospects”.

propositions.text: Ms Soni flagpoled once, was refused work permit April 2, received Visitor Record, reapplied April 10, refused again, then received Authorization to Leave and complied.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni: … flagpoled once, was refused a WP at the border on April 2, received a VR and re-applied again on April 10, 2019. She was again refused and eventually received an ATL, with which I note she complied.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Officer’s GCMS Notes detailed Ms Soni’s migration history and border work permit attempts.

propositions.text: Officer was aware of non-disclosure concern at border on March 26 and Ms Soni’s explanations in declaration and counsel’s letter.
propositions.quote: The Officer was clearly aware of the events at issue and the non-disclosure concern ... as identified by the Peace Bridge Officer ... which Ms Soni sought to explain in her Statutory Declaration. Her legal counsel’s letter reiterated her explanation

propositions.text: Officer likely read counsel’s letter or declaration to identify non-disclosure of employment prospects.
propositions.quote: It is also not clear from the record how the Officer would have identified the non-disclosure ... unless the Officer had read counsel’s letter or her Statutory Declaration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer knew of the non-disclosure concern and Ms Soni’s explanations, likely from counsel’s letter or declaration.

propositions.text: Officer noted Ms Soni complied with requirement to exit Canada on April 29, a fact favoring her.
propositions.quote: the Officer recognized that Ms Soni complied with the requirement to exit Canada on April 29. That must have been a fact in favour of Ms Soni

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Officer recognized Ms Soni complied with exit requirements, favoring her case.

propositions.text: Officer was aware family would travel together; GCMS Notes refer to three visa applications at start and end.
propositions.quote: the Officer was also aware from the record that the family would travel together. The Officer’s GCMS Notes refer to three applications for visas both at the outset and at the end.

propositions.text: Court will return to Ms Soni’s position on this third element later.
propositions.quote: I will return below to Ms Soni’s position on this third element.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer knew the family would travel together and notes three visa applications; will revisit Ms Soni’s position.

propositions.text: These three elements and circumstances led Officer to conclude Ms Soni was not a bona fide temporary resident under IRPR 200(1)(b).
propositions.quote: It is these three elements and the stated circumstances that led the Officer to conclude that “I am not satisfied ... that the applicant would be a bona fide temporary resident

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer concluded Ms Soni was not a bona fide temporary resident based on these three elements.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes identified discrepancies and non-disclosure in Ms Soni’s migration history, central to Officer’s reasoning.
propositions.quote: the GCMS Notes clearly identified the “discrepancies” and the “non-disclosure” in Ms Soni’s migration history. In my view, that was at the heart of the Officer’s reasoning

propositions.text: Officer’s reference to concerns after counsel’s letter refers to discrepancies.
propositions.quote: there is also no other way to read the Officer’s reference to the “concerns” that remained after reading counsel’s letter (recognizing that at that point, the Officer appears only to be referring to the “discrepancies”).

propositions.text: Peace Bridge Officer also recognized and articulated these concerns to Ms Soni on April 11.
propositions.quote: the Peace Bridge Officer in Canada had also recognized and articulated those same concerns to Ms Soni on April 11.

propositions.text: Ms Soni swore Statutory Declaration addressing concerns in detail less than a week later.
propositions.quote: Less than a week later, while still in Canada, she swore the Statutory Declaration that addressed them in detail.

propositions.text: She retained Canadian counsel who summarized evidence and made submissions addressing concerns.
propositions.quote: She retained Canadian counsel who summarized all the evidence to support her work permit application and made submissions on her behalf to address those very concerns.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds discrepancies and non-disclosure central to Officer’s reasoning; Ms Soni addressed concerns in declaration and counsel’s submissions.

propositions.text: Applicant contends Officer failed to engage sufficiently with sworn explanations and should have accepted them.
propositions.quote: The applicant contends that the Officer failed to engage sufficiently with her explanations given under oath and should have given effect to them

propositions.text: Respondent argues Ms Soni lied twice and Officer had right to refuse work permit on that basis alone.
propositions.quote: the respondent argues that it is simple: Ms Soni lied, twice, and the Officer had the legal right to refuse her work permit application on that basis alone.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues Officer failed to engage with sworn explanations; respondent says Ms Soni lied and refusal was justified.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with both parties; Officer did not find Ms Soni lied intentionally.
propositions.quote: I do not agree completely with either party. I agree with the applicant that the GCMS Notes do not state that Ms Soni lied

propositions.text: Issue for Officer was whether Ms Soni would leave Canada by end of authorized stay under IRPR 200(1)(b).
propositions.quote: The issue for the Officer was whether Ms Soni would leave Canada by the end of the period authorized for her stay in the requested work permit, under IRPR paragraph 2001(1)(b).

propositions.text: Sufficient for Officer to consider non-disclosure and discrepancies as factors in assessing whether Ms Soni would exit Canada.
propositions.quote: it was sufficient for the Officer to recognize ... the matters expressly stated in the GCMS Notes – her migration history included “not disclosing her employment prospects” ... and the factual “discrepancies”

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer did not say Ms Soni lied but reasonably considered non-disclosure and discrepancies to assess if she would leave Canada.

propositions.text: Respondent says past interactions with immigration officials are relevant to assessment under IRPR 200(1)(b).
propositions.quote: Ms Soni’s past interactions with Canadian immigration officials are generally relevant to the Officer’s assessment under paragraph 200(1)(b)

propositions.text: Respondent argues Officer entitled to consider truthfulness or lack thereof in decision to grant or refuse work permit.
propositions.quote: the Officer was entitled to take into account Ms Soni’s truthfulness on relevant matters ... when making a decision to grant or refuse the work permit

propositions.text: Cites cases supporting relevance of past interactions and truthfulness in assessing temporary residence.
propositions.quote: see Calaunan v. Canada ... Obeng v. Canada ... Ngalamulume v Canada ... Porfirio ... Chamma ... Mescallado ... Barud ...

propositions.text: Court agrees with respondent that truthfulness is relevant under IRPA s.16 and case law in assessing leave to Canada.
propositions.quote: I agree with the respondent that the Officer was entitled to take into account Ms Soni’s truthfulness ... under the IRPA, when making a decision ... under paragraph 200(1)(b)

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues and court agrees that past interactions and truthfulness are relevant to assessing temporary residence under IRPR 200(1)(b).

propositions.text: Court finds Officer was not legally or factually required to accept Ms Soni’s explanations in declaration or letters.
propositions.quote: I am unable to conclude ... that the Officer was required ... to accept the explanations in Ms Soni’s Statutory Declaration ... Her explanations did not operate as a constraint on the Officer

propositions.text: Officer expressly stated considering counsel’s letter but concerns remained.
propositions.quote: The Officer expressly stated that he or she had considered legal counsel’s letter that contained those explanations, but the officer’s concerns remained.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer was not required to accept Ms Soni’s explanations and had considered counsel’s letter but remained concerned.

propositions.text: Court’s role is not to reassess or reweigh evidence on judicial review: Vavilov para 125.
propositions.quote: That is not the role of a court on a judicial review application: Vavilov, at para 125.

propositions.text: Ms Soni asks court to reassess evidence about signed visa application errors and non-disclosure, which is improper.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni is asking the Court to reassess or reweigh the evidence of her submitting a signed visa application that contained admitted errors ... That is not the role of a court

paragraphs.summary: The court states it cannot reassess or reweigh evidence on judicial review, rejecting Ms Soni’s request to do so.

propositions.text: Officer sufficiently understood and considered evidence and arguments by Ms Soni and counsel.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Officer sufficiently understood and considered the evidence and the central arguments made by Ms Soni and her counsel

propositions.text: This is not a case where decision-maker ignored or misapprehended evidence making decision untenable.
propositions.quote: This is not a case where a decision-maker ignored, fundamentally misapprehended or failed to account for evidence so as to render the decision “untenable”.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer properly considered evidence and arguments and did not ignore or misapprehend evidence.

propositions.text: Applicant referred to many court decisions, including Xie where failure to consider declaration led to setting aside decision.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s submissions referred to numerous decisions of this Court. I will address two in particular. In Xie ... the applicant filed a declaration ... An Officer failed to consider the declaration and Justice Pinard set aside the decision on judicial review.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant cited cases including Xie where failure to consider declaration led to decision being set aside.

propositions.text: Xie is distinguishable because it involved an express sworn statement of intent to leave Canada with supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: The Court in Xie, and in the cases it considered, was concerned with statements that an applicant would leave the country at the end of a permitted stay.

propositions.text: Mr Xie expressly stated in a sworn declaration he would return to China and provided supporting evidence.
propositions.quote: In his case, Mr Xie expressly stated in a sworn declaration that he would return to China at the end of his permitted stay in Canada and provided supporting evidence to explain why.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Xie distinguishable because Mr Xie made an express sworn statement and provided supporting evidence about leaving Canada.

propositions.text: Ms Soni made no express statement in her Statutory Declaration about leaving Canada.
propositions.quote: First, Ms Soni made no such express statement in her Statutory Declaration.

propositions.text: It is unclear how such a statement might have affected the Officer's decision on her work permit.
propositions.quote: It is not possible to say whether or how such a statement and explanation – assuming she could have provided them – might ultimately have affected the Officer’s decision on her work permit application.

propositions.text: Applicant's Statutory Declaration does not address ties to India or reasons for return.
propositions.quote: In addition, unlike Xie, the applicant’s Statutory Declaration does not address the applicant’s or her husband’s ties to India or any other reasons why she or the family will return to India at the end of her requested work permit.

propositions.text: Applicant does not argue Officer failed to consider such evidence and none appears in her Statutory Declaration.
propositions.quote: The applicant does not argue that the Officer failed to consider this kind of evidence and no such evidence appears in her Statutory Declaration.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ms Soni made no express statement about leaving Canada and her declaration lacks evidence of ties to India or reasons to return.

propositions.text: Aghaalikhani is unlike this case because there was no evidence supporting the Officer's views about ties to Canada.
propositions.quote: In Aghaalikhani, Justice Gascon held that there was no evidence to support the Officer’s views that the applicant had ties to Canada and would therefore not leave at the end of a study permit.

propositions.text: Justice Gascon found Officer's reasons incomprehensible and arbitrary due to lack of evidence.
propositions.quote: He concluded that the Officer’s reasons were incomprehensible because there was “no evidence on the record to support them and they appear to be completely arbitrary in light of the evidence submitted” (at para 26).

propositions.text: Justice Gascon identified irrationality, arbitrariness, illogic and baseless factual findings in Aghaalikhani.
propositions.quote: See also his references to irrationality, arbitrariness, illogic and “factual findings without any basis whatsoever” in paragraph 17.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Aghaalikhani unlike this case because the Officer's views lacked evidentiary support and were arbitrary.

propositions.text: There is evidence supporting Officer's concerns about Ms Soni's truthfulness in interactions with immigration officials.
propositions.quote: By contrast, in this case there is evidence in the record here to support the Officer’s concerns about the truthfulness of Ms Soni’s interactions with immigration officials.

propositions.text: Ms Soni's Statutory Declaration was an attempt to explain discrepancies and non-disclosure at the border.
propositions.quote: The explanations in her Statutory Declaration, which she submits were ignored, were not the only evidence on the issue – they were her attempt to explain away the “discrepancies” and the non-disclosure at the border.

propositions.text: Based on GCMS Notes, Officer did not disregard material in the work permit application.
propositions.quote: Based on the GCMS Notes, I am satisfied that the Officer did not disregard the material in the work permit application.

propositions.text: No concerns about arbitrariness or irrationality as identified in Aghaalikhani.
propositions.quote: In addition, I do not have the same underlying concerns about arbitrariness or irrationality identified by Justice Gascon in Aghaalikhani.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence supports Officer's concerns about Ms Soni's truthfulness and no arbitrariness or irrationality exists here.

propositions.text: Officer's consideration of Ms Soni's repeated attempts to obtain a work permit at the border is ambiguous but not a mere recitation of fact.
propositions.quote: The respondent characterized it as a “mere recitation” of fact. I do not think so.

propositions.text: Ms Soni's efforts to apply for a work permit at ports of entry involved errors, some beyond her control.
propositions.quote: As explained in her Statutory Declaration and through the supporting documents such as her DHL courier receipt, Ms Soni’s efforts to apply for a work permit at the ports of entry in April 2019 became something of a comedy of errors, with some elements out of her control.

propositions.text: Even accepting Ms Soni's position, Officer's overall decision remains reasonable under Vavilov standards.
propositions.quote: However, in the end, even accepting her position on this issue would not render the Officer’s overall decision untenable or unreasonable on Vavilov standards.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer's consideration of Ms Soni's attempts at the border is ambiguous but not mere fact recital; decision remains reasonable.

propositions.text: Officer inferred that family traveling together suggests Ms Soni would not leave family behind in India.
propositions.quote: The Officer must have considered their travel together as some evidence that Ms Soni would not be leaving her immediate family behind in India in order to pursue the work opportunity in Canada.

propositions.text: It is proper to consider family travel together when determining if applicant will leave Canada under IRPR 200(1)(b).
propositions.quote: It is hard to see how it is improper to do so when determining whether she would leave Canada at the end of her permitted stay under IRPR paragraph 200(1)(b).

propositions.text: If family did not come to Canada, ties remaining in India would be relevant to departure determination.
propositions.quote: Consider the converse – if the evidence were that her husband and son did not propose to come to Canada during her intended work period, those personal ties remaining in India would surely have been relevant to the determination of whether she would leave as required.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it proper for Officer to infer family travel together suggests Ms Soni would not leave family behind in India.

propositions.text: Officer's decision was reasonable.
propositions.quote: For these reasons, I conclude that the Officer’s decision was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer's decision was reasonable.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requires knowing the case to meet and meaningful opportunity to respond.
propositions.quote: Procedural fairness requires that a party know the case to meet and have a meaningful opportunity to respond to it.

propositions.text: Ms Soni argues she should have been given opportunity to respond if Officer had concerns about her Statutory Declaration.
propositions.quote: Ms Soni submitted that if the Officer had concerns about her sworn Statutory Declaration, she should have been given an opportunity to respond.

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness requires notice and response opportunity; Ms Soni argues she should have been allowed to respond to concerns.

propositions.text: Officer provided procedural fairness; Ms Soni had opportunity to respond and did so.
propositions.quote: I do not believe that the Officer failed to provide the applicant with procedural fairness in this case. In fact, she had an opportunity to respond and well availed herself of it.

propositions.text: Concerns identified by Officer were same as those raised by Peace Bridge Officer on April 11, 2019.
propositions.quote: The concerns identified by the Officer in the GCMS Notes were the same as those identified to Ms Soni by the Peace Bridge Officer at that port of entry on April 11, 2019.

propositions.text: Ms Soni addressed issues in Statutory Declaration and counsel's May 10, 2019 letter, both submitted for Officer's consideration.
propositions.quote: She addressed those issues in her Statutory Declaration sworn in Canada a week later. Her counsel advocated on those issues in their May 10, 2019 letter. Both were submitted for the Officer’s consideration.

propositions.text: Officer was not required to provide Ms Soni with additional opportunity to respond.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Officer was not required to provide Ms Soni with an additional kick at the same can.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Officer provided procedural fairness; Ms Soni had ample opportunity to respond and no further chance was required.

propositions.text: Applicant's submission on inadequacy of reasons overlaps with unreasonableness arguments; court will focus on adequacy points.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s submission that the Officer’s reasons were inadequate overlapped significantly with her arguments on unreasonableness generally. I will try to focus on the different points made about the adequacy of the reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes applicant's inadequacy submission overlaps with unreasonableness and will focus on adequacy points.

propositions.text: LeBon involved denial of transfer request despite unequivocal CSC opinion supporting transfer.
propositions.quote: In that case, the applicant was incarcerated outside Canada. The Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness denied his request for a transfer to Canada and he unsuccessfully applied to this Court for judicial review.

propositions.text: Federal Court of Appeal allowed appeal and set aside Minister's denial of transfer in LeBon.
propositions.quote: Justice Dawson, speaking for the Federal Court of Appeal, allowed an appeal and set aside the Minister’s denial of a transfer.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes LeBon where the Federal Court of Appeal set aside Minister's denial of transfer despite CSC's support.

propositions.text: No bright line test for level of explanation when Minister disagrees with advice; depends on record.
propositions.quote: Justice Dawson, speaking for the Federal Court of Appeal, allowed an appeal and set aside the Minister’s denial of a transfer.

propositions.text: In LeBon, Minister disagreed with CSC's opinion without cogent evidence undermining it, making conclusion unjustified.
propositions.quote: In some cases, little or no explanation may be required because the record may make it apparent why the Minister disagreed. However, in LeBon, counsel on the appeal could not point to any cogent evidence in the record that would reasonably undermine or contradict the CSC’s opinion.

propositions.text: Minister's conclusion was not justified, transparent or intelligible in LeBon.
propositions.quote: “the conclusion reached was not justified, transparent or intelligible:” see LeBon, at paras 20 and 23.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains LeBon's rule that Minister must justify disagreement with advice; failure made decision unjustified and unintelligible.

propositions.text: Minister required by statute to provide written reasons explaining assessment of competing factors in LeBon.
propositions.quote: Justice Dawson held that the statute required the Minister to do more than assert that the unique facts and circumstances had been considered in the context of the legal test.

propositions.text: Without explanation of competing factors, decision is not transparent, intelligible, or compliant with statutory reasons requirement.
propositions.quote: If there were factors that support the requested transfer, the Minister had to demonstrate “some assessment of the competing factors so as to explain why he refused to consent to the transfer” – without which the decision is neither transparent nor intelligible and would not comply with the statutory requirement to give reasons: LeBon, at para 25.

paragraphs.summary: The court states LeBon requires Minister to explain competing factors to meet statutory reasons requirement.

propositions.text: Iyiola involved a study visa case where Officer's sparse notes failed to articulate intelligibly why applicant was not genuine student.
propositions.quote: Justice Fuhrer concluded that an Officer did not articulate intelligibly or reasonably why Mr Iyiola was not considered a genuine student (at para 19)

propositions.text: Officer's decision in Iyiola was unintelligible for failing to address family ties and absence of spouse or foreign travel.
propositions.quote: On the latter, the Officer’s decision was unintelligible for failure to deal with the applicant’s significant family ties in his home country and why the absence of a spouse or prior documented foreign travel would be factors against a student visa.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes Iyiola where Officer's reasons were unintelligible for failing to address family ties and travel history.

propositions.text: Unlike LeBon, this case did not involve unequivocal opinion or one-sided facts leading to single conclusion.
propositions.quote: In contrast with LeBon, the decision-maker in this case was not faced with an unequivocal opinion or a one-sided set of facts that could lead to a single conclusion.

propositions.text: Officer had to decide whether to accept Ms Soni's explanations for inconsistencies and border communications.
propositions.quote: The Officer had to decide whether to accept Ms Soni’s explanations for the admitted inconsistencies between her TRV application and her work permit application, and for the communications at the border on March 26 related to the purposes of that trip.

propositions.text: Officer's concerns related to Ms Soni's truthfulness with immigration officials.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s concerns went to Ms Soni’s truthfulness in interactions with immigration officials.

propositions.text: No evidence of ties to India or Canada to weigh as in Iyiola.
propositions.quote: Nor did the Officer need to weigh evidence of various factors that might tie Ms Soni and her family to India or to Canada as in Iyiola – as already noted, there was no such evidence.

propositions.text: GCMS Notes provide sufficient insight into Officer's conclusion Ms Soni would not leave Canada under IRPR 200(1)(b).
propositions.quote: the GCMS Notes shed sufficient insight into why the Officer concluded that Ms Soni would not leave Canada at the end of her authorized stay under IRPR paragraph 200(1)(b).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case differs from LeBon and Iyiola; Officer's concerns about truthfulness and GCMS Notes provide sufficient insight.

propositions.text: Reasons in this case do not suffer from flaws identified in Aghaalikhani.
propositions.quote: For the reasons already stated, the reasons in the present case do not suffer from the same flaws as Justice Gascon identified in Aghaalikhani.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds reasons here do not have the flaws identified in Aghaalikhani.

propositions.text: No basis to set aside Officer's decision for inadequate reasons.
propositions.quote: I conclude that there is no basis to set aside the Officer’s decision on the basis that the reasons were inadequate.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes there is no basis to set aside the Officer's decision for inadequate reasons.

propositions.text: Officer refused study permit for Ms Soni's son as consequence of refusal of Ms Soni's work permit.
propositions.quote: the Officer at the High Commission refused the application for a study permit made on behalf of Ms Soni’s son, Viren Nimeshbhai Soni, expressly as a consequence of the refusal of his mother’s application for a work permit.

propositions.text: No indication that son's or husband's applications were considered or refused on their own merits.
propositions.quote: Nothing in the letter from the High Commission or in the Officer’s GCMS Notes suggests that the application for Viren’s study permit was either considered, or refused, on its own merits. The same may be said about the application of Ms Soni’s husband, Nimeshkumar Dhirubhai Soni.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the son's and husband's applications were refused as consequence of Ms Soni's refusal, not on their own merits.

propositions.text: Application for judicial review is dismissed; no question certified; no costs ordered.
propositions.quote: The application is dismissed. Neither party proposed a question for certification and none arises. This is not a case for costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application, declines certification, and orders no costs.
